title: Next Arrangement Up
statement:
Think of every possible ordering of the numbers in nums, sorted like words in a dictionary (compare the first entries, then the second, and so on). Rearrange nums in place into the ordering that comes right after the current one.

If the current ordering is already the last one (the numbers are in non-increasing order), wrap around to the first: the numbers in non-decreasing order.

nums may contain repeated values; orderings that look the same count once. Use O(1) extra memory and return nothing. The checker reads nums afterwards.

examples.why: The tail [4, 3, 1] is already as high as it can go, so the 2 must grow. It is replaced by the smallest bigger value to its right, 3 (not 4), and the tail is then made as low as possible.
This is the last ordering, so it wraps around to the first one.
Swapping the two 5s changes nothing, so it is not the next ordering. The 1 has to move.

hints: To get the very next ordering, change as little as possible, and as far to the right as possible. When can the last few numbers not be rearranged into anything bigger?
Scan from the right for the first index i with nums[i] < nums[i + 1]. Everything after i is non-increasing, so it is already at its maximum; nums[i] is the number that must grow.

Swap nums[i] with the rightmost value after it that is bigger than nums[i]. The tail is still non-increasing, so reverse it to make it the smallest possible. If no such i exists, just reverse the whole array.

explain.intuition:
Think of the array like a number on a car odometer: the next reading changes the rightmost digit that can still go up. A tail that is non-increasing (like 4, 3, 1) is already the biggest arrangement of its values, so nothing inside it can go up. The first number to the left of that tail, the pivot, is the one that must grow.

It should grow by as little as possible, so swap it with the smallest value in the tail that is bigger than it. Because the tail is sorted high to low, that value is the rightmost one bigger than the pivot, and the tail stays sorted high to low after the swap. Finally, the tail should be as small as possible: reversing it turns high-to-low into low-to-high.
steps: If there is none, reverse the whole array and stop.
Find the largest j > i with nums[j] > nums[i], and swap nums[i] with nums[j].
pitfalls: Swapping the pivot with the largest value in the tail instead of the smallest bigger one. [2, 4, 3, 1] would become [4, ...] and skip over the orderings starting with 3.
Using ≤ vs < wrongly with duplicates. The pivot needs a strictly bigger right neighbour, and the swap partner must be strictly bigger than the pivot.
Sorting the tail instead of reversing it. It works but costs O(n log n) for no reason.

solutions.title: Walk orderings in dictionary order
solutions.idea: Generate distinct orderings of the sorted values in dictionary order and stop at the first one bigger than nums. Fall back to the sorted order if there is none. Only usable for tiny inputs.

solutions.title: Pivot, swap, reverse
solutions.idea: Find the rightmost number that can grow, raise it to the next bigger value from its right, and make everything after it as small as possible.
